title: OpenFilm's one rule: the same t always draws the same frame
summary: OpenFilm's one rule for agent-made video: the same t always draws the same frame. Each shot is a web page with frame(t), and openfilm look draws its contact sheet twice in shuffled orders to flag changed frames: https://github.com/openfilm/openfilm
body_markdown:
OpenFilm, an open-source AI video agent and editor, puts its effort into checking the films coding agents make. Each page in a film follows one rule: the same `t` always draws the same picture, whatever was drawn before.

The checker in openfilm/openfilm is built around that rule.

## A film is a folder with a film.html

A film is a `film.html` file holding tracks of clips. Each `<section>` is a track, with the first one on top in the timeline. A clip is an element, which can be a page, a video, a still picture or a sound:

```html
<section>
  <video src="assets/footage.mp4#t=12,18" at="4" speed="0.5" class="card"></video>
</section>
```

Which part of a file plays is a media fragment like `#t=12,18`, where it starts is `at`, where it sits is its CSS position, and how it looks is CSS. The pitch is that your agent already knows the web, so there is nothing new for it to learn.

Each shot is a web page that exposes one function:

```js
window.film = {
  frame(t) { /* draw the complete picture at t seconds */ },
  duration: 4,
  ready: loadFonts(),
};
```

Inside `frame(t)` you can use anything a browser can draw: three.js, WebGL, canvas, SVG, CSS, GSAP or video. There is no framework on top. The project names Remotion and HyperFrames as the frameworks it avoids, on the view that one function is enough. Anything made outside the browser, such as Blender output or a video model's clips, comes in as video or images.

## Why the one rule matters

Frames are requested out of order, in parallel, and between frames for motion blur. A page that keeps state between calls, say an animation that advances a counter each time it draws, will render differently depending on which frames were asked for first. Keep the rule and a page renders the same at any size on any machine.

That is also how OpenFilm checks the agent's work. The project says it spends its effort where models fail, on checking the film. The `look` command draws every frame of its contact sheet twice, in two shuffled orders, and names any frame that changed. It also reports page errors, fonts that failed to load, missing sound files, and text cut off by the frame. An agent can run it after an edit and get a concrete list of what broke.

## You can still edit it by hand

Studio, the local editor, runs in a Chromium-based browser because that is the engine films are drawn and exported with, so the preview matches the export. You can move, scale and rotate elements inside a page, change text, colour and style, and trim and cut clips on the timeline. Your edits are saved to the film's files, with changes to elements inside a page kept as `overrides`, and agents keep them when they edit later.

Export covers MP4 with options for 4K, motion blur and loudness targets, plus GIF, stems, subtitles, transparent video, and timelines for Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve. A canvas beside the edit lets you and the agent lay out notes, clips, voice-over and music before sending them to the timeline.

How a kind of film gets made lives in skills, not in the tool, and community skills install from openfilm/skills.

## Making a first film

You need Node 22.2+ and ffmpeg. The first run downloads a headless Chromium of about 100 MB.

```sh
npx skills add openfilm/openfilm
```

Then ask your agent for something like "a 20-second launch video for my CLI, with music". Making, editing and rendering need no account. For generated voice, music and images, you either connect services with your own keys or sign in to OpenFilm. I would run `openfilm look` on the first draft before watching it, and see what it flags.
